Overview

ColonyPy automates the counting and classification of fungal colonies on petri dish images. It uses a trained StarDist deep-learning model to detect individual colonies, measures their size, and classifies each colony as either:

  • Tolerance smaller than the control-derived 25th percentile (p25) colony size (grows under drug pressure)
  • Heteroresistance same size or larger than the control p25 (potentially resistant sub-population)

The classification threshold is derived automatically from matching control plates (no-drug) using the same strain. No manual threshold setting is required when control plates are present.

The trained StarDist model is included in the model_data/ folder and loads automatically when ColonyPy starts. You do not need to attach or download any model file separately.

Launching ColonyPy

ColonyPy is distributed as a standalone executable built with PyInstaller. No Python installation, no command line, and no internet connection are required on the user's machine. Everything including the trained StarDist model and all dependencies is bundled inside the executable.

Platform Performance

macOS and Linux are strongly recommended. Both are natively compatible with the machine learning libraries ColonyPy uses and analyse a typical plate image in approximately 20 seconds.

Windows is supported but has known compatibility limitations with machine learning frameworks. On Windows, a single image may take 3–5 minutes to analyse. If you are on Windows and need faster performance, the recommended solution is to set up Ubuntu via WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) and run the Linux version of ColonyPy, this restores the ~20 second per image speed. Instructions: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install.

Windows

Double-click ColonyPy.exe

Windows may show a SmartScreen warning on first launch. Click More info → Run anyway.

macOS

Double-click ColonyPy.app

On first launch, right-click → Open → Open. You may need to allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security.

Linux

Run ./ColonyPy/ColonyPy from a terminal, or double-click if your file manager supports it.

No Setup Required

The executable is entirely self-contained. There is no installation step and no internet connection needed to run ColonyPy.

First Launch Slow Start
On the very first launch, the executable may take 5-10 minutes to start while it unpacks its bundled libraries. Subsequent launches are faster. This is normal behaviour for PyInstaller executables.

Imaging Requirements

For reliable colony detection, images must match the conditions used to train the StarDist model. Deviation from these conditions will reduce detection accuracy.

ParameterRequired ValueNotes
BackgroundWhite transillumination trayTray must be clean as residue causes false detections
ImagerBio-Rad ChemiDocWhite transillumination mode
Exposure0.9 secondsStandard setting. Use this for all imaging. Only adjust if you observe poor colony contrast with your specific media. See guidance below.
Image sizeMedium (ChemiDoc setting)1830 × 1646 pixels
Resolution300 DPIBoth axes
Bit depth24-bit colour8-bit per RGB channel
Physical size15.5 × 12.4 cmAt the Medium image setting
Plate size90 mm petri dishStandard round plate
Export formatJPEG or PNG or TIFFDo not resize images before importing
Do Not Resize
Never resize or resample images before importing into ColonyPy. The pixel-to-mm calibration assumes the original ChemiDoc dimensions (1830 × 1646 px, 300 DPI). Resizing invalidates the calibration and produces incorrect colony size measurements.

ChemiDoc Export Settings

When exporting from the ChemiDoc Image Lab software, use these exact settings:

  1. Select File → Export Image
  2. Set image size to Medium
  3. Resolution: 300 DPI
  4. Format: JPEG (high quality) or PNG
    5. or TIFF
  5. Do not apply any post-processing filters before export

Adjusting Exposure for Different Media

0.9 seconds is the standard exposure and should work correctly for the vast majority of plates. Only consider adjusting if you image a plate and observe clearly poor contrast. For example colonies that are nearly invisible, or a background so bright that colonies cannot be distinguished. If adjustment is needed, stay within the 0.8–1.5 second range and use the reference images below as your target.

Target Contrast Goal

At 0.9 s, most plates will already look like the reference images below. If yours do not, use these two criteria to judge whether an exposure adjustment is needed:

  • Colonies appear as clearly distinct bright spots against a dark agar background
  • The agar background is uniformly dark with no large bright patches or blown-out regions

Reference Images, What Good Contrast Looks Like

Use these images as a visual benchmark when setting your exposure. Both were acquired on a Bio-Rad ChemiDoc with Coomassie Blue lighting.

Disk Diffusion Plate

Good contrast: dense uniform colony ring clearly visible against a dark ZOI interior. Individual colonies are distinguishable as separate white dots at the outer edge. The antifungal disk appears as a bright white central circle.

Agar dilution Plate

Good contrast: colonies appear as bright, well-separated white spots on a uniformly dark background. Colonies near the rim are fully visible. No blown-out regions or bright background patches.

If and Only If Contrast Is Poor: Adjustment Tips
  • Background too bright / colonies hard to distinguish → reduce exposure (try 0.85,0.8 s)
  • Colonies very dim or invisible against background → increase exposure (try 0.95,1.0,1.1–1.5 s)
  • Colonies appear blown out (pure white, no edge detail) → reduce exposure
  • Always capture a test image first and compare it visually to the reference plates above before imaging your full batch
  • Once you find the right exposure for a media type, record it and use it consistently across all plates in that experiment
Consistency Within a Run
Once you choose an exposure setting, do not change it between a control plate and its matching test plates. Each control plate and its associated test plates must be imaged at the same exposure as the threshold calibration derived from the control applies only to plates imaged under identical conditions. Different plate types within the same run may require different exposure settings, provided each control is matched to its corresponding test plates at the same setting.

What Bad Contrast Looks Like. Do Not Use

Images like these will produce poor detection results:

Uneven Lighting, Agar Dilution Plate

Colonies are visible but uneven lighting for example brighter near the rim, lighter patches in the plate, causes inconsistent thresholding and missed or false-positive detections.

Confluent Growth, Disk Diffusion Plate

Uneven lighting with lighter patches in the ZOI causes false positive detection.

Good Practice Guidelines

Inoculum Preparation

Critical: Control Plate Inoculum Concentration

ColonyPy uses StarDist, a convex shape detection model. It is designed to detect convex colonies. It cannot detect colonies within confluent lawns.

Using too high an inoculum in strain control plates will cause:

  • Unreliable threshold calibration from control plates

Recommended practice:

  • Optimise inoculum concentration so that colonies on the control plate are well-separated
  • Control plates should produce distinct, non-overlapping colonies across the whole plate
  • Aim for 100-500 countable colonies per plate
  • Dutring testing, if the ZOI shows a lawn, dilute the inoculum and repeat

Plate Preparation

  • Use standard 90 mm round petri dishes, any other sizes require parameter adjustment
  • Ensure the tray is clean before imaging. Residue on the tray creates bright spots that may be detected as colonies
  • Place only one plate per image. ColonyPy analyses one plate per image file
  • Remove the plate lid before imaging
  • Ensure the plate is upright, resting on its bottom, with the agar surface facing up
  • Do not image plates with writing on the bottom or along the sides, as markings interfere with analysis
  • Ensure the plate is centred and fully in frame with no shadows cut across it

Critical: Plate Cleanliness

  • The agar surface, plate rim and plate bottom must be free of artefacts, bubbles, condensation, or media residue. Any dark marks near the plate edge can disrupt the plate-boundary detection algorithm.

Re-run and Overwrite Policy

Important: Output Directory Policy

ColonyPy writes results into the output directory you specify. If you re-run an analysis with the same output directory, the relevant results CSV (colony_analysis_results.csv for disk diffusion, agar_dilution_results.csv for agar dilution) is overwritten for any image that is re-processed.

Best practice: always use a new, separate output directory for each re-run. This preserves your original results and avoids accidental data loss. Use clear naming such as:

  • results_2025-06-01_run1/
  • results_2025-06-01_run2_adjusted_ZOI/

File Naming Convention

Correct file naming is essential for ColonyPy to match control plates to test plates of the same strain and to group replicates for statistics.

What happens if naming is wrong? Files will be listed as invalid and skipped entirely, no error will be shown for individual files, the run will just produce no results.

Plate TypeFormatExample
Control plate{strain}_C.jpgKN99_C.jpg
Test plate{strain}_rep{n}_{condition}.jpgKN99_rep1_FLC.jpg
  • Control plates must end with _C (case-insensitive) before the file extension
  • The strain identifier must match between control and test plates
  • Conditions and replicate numbers are used for grouping statistics
  • Supported formats: .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .bmp, .tiff, .tif
  • Control plates are identified by their filename ending in _C before the extension, for example KN99_C.jpg. A replicate number is optional for example, KN99_rep1_C.jpg also works, but KN99_C.jpg is sufficient.

What actually happens when a run is performed without controls?

In Agar dilution mode

  • If no control plates exist at all in the folder → analysis stops immediately with "No control plates found" and returns no results
  • If a control exists for some strains but not others → test plates for the unmatched strains are silently skipped with a console message only; they won't appear in output or CSV
  • If a control plate is present but colony detection fails on it → that strain's threshold falls back to the hardcoded default of 12 px, and percentages will be 0%

In Disk diffusion mode

  • If no control plates exist at all in the folder → analysis will proceed and all test strain threshold falls back to the hardcoded default of 12 px
  • If a control exists for some strains but not others → test plates for the unmatched strains threshold will use the default 12 px, while matched test plates will utilise control colony p25 threshold

Analysis Tab Step by Step

Pre-Analysis Check

The Analysis tab shows four green ticks when everything is ready:

  • ✅ Input directory selected
  • ✅ Output directory selected
  • ✅ Analysis method chosen
  • ✅ Images found in directory

If any item shows ✗, go back to Setup and correct it. Click Refresh Check to revalidate after making changes.

Analysis Options

OptionDescription
Create comparison plotsGenerate annotated PDF for each image. Recommended to leave enabled.
Save CSV resultsAppend each image result to colony_analysis_results.csv (disk diffusion) or agar_dilution_results.csv (agar dilution), whichever matches the selected analysis method. Leave enabled.
Max replicates per PDFControls how many replicates appear in comparison PDFs. Default 4.
Enhanced DetectionUses the 95th percentile instead of 99.8th for StarDist normalisation. Improves detection of dim, small, or densely packed colonies. See guidance below before enabling.
Enhanced Detection. When to Use

Enhanced Detection lowers the upper normalisation percentile from 99.8th to 95th before model inference, boosting dim or small colonies so the model can pick them up. It is off by default and is a per-plate decision , enable it on any plate, any mode, where many colonies are being missed. Do not apply it to plates where standard detection is already working well, as using it on a well-imaged plate risks oversegmentation and false positives.

SituationRecommendation
Many colonies missed on a plate Enable Enhanced Detection for that plate regardless of mode (disk diffusion, agar dilution, or control). Check the result in the Manual Editor, if you see colonies being split or false positives appearing, revert to standard.
Detection already looks good on a plate Leave Enhanced Detection off. Enabling it unnecessarily on a well-imaged plate can cause oversegmentation.

Starting Analysis

  1. Click Start Analysis
  2. A dialog asks you to choose your workflow:
    • YES Manual review: After each image is automatically analysed, the Manual Editor opens for you to correct detections. Best accuracy. Recommended for publications.
    • NO Fully automated: All images are processed without review. Faster, suitable for screening.
    • CANCEL: Abort and return to the main window.
  3. Watch progress in the log area. Control plates are processed first to establish baselines.
  4. When complete, the Results tab opens automatically.

To halt a running analysis, click Stop Analysis. Already-processed images are saved; the analysis can be resumed later.

Resuming an Interrupted Analysis

If analysis is interrupted (stopped or crashes), relaunch ColonyPy, select the same input and output directories, and click Start Analysis. ColonyPy detects which images were already processed from the existing CSV and asks if you want to resume. Click YES to skip already-completed images.

Manual Boundary Adjustments

Occasionally the automatic boundary detection is imprecise. The editor provides sliders to correct this before re-detecting colonies.

Adjusting the ZOI Boundary (Disk Diffusion)

The ZOI (Zone of Inhibition) boundary is the circle around the disk within which colonies are counted. If it is too tight or too wide:

  1. In the Manual Editor left panel, find the ZOI Boundary slider
  2. Drag the slider left to shrink the ZOI or right to expand it
  3. The yellow dashed arc on the image updates in real time
  4. Click Re-detect Colonies to rerun StarDist detection with the new boundary
Re-detection
When you click Re-detect Colonies, the full analysis pipeline (sharpening → CLAHE → reference standardisation → StarDist) runs again with your new boundary. This is identical to the original automated analysis not a simple filter of old results.

Adjusting the Disk Size

If the disk detection is slightly off (disk circle too large or too small over the actual disk):

  1. Find the Disk Radius slider in the editor left panel
  2. Adjust until the grey disk overlay matches the physical disk in the image
  3. Click Re-detect Colonies colonies that overlap the disk exclusion zone will be removed

Adjusting the Plate Boundary

The green circle should sit precisely on the inner edge of the petri dish rim. If it is too large (picking up false colonies on the rim) or too small (missing edge colonies):

  1. Find the Plate Radius slider in the editor left panel
  2. Drag left to shrink the boundary (excludes more rim) or right to expand it
  3. For agar dilution plates where the rim is thick or falsely bright, shrink the plate radius until the green circle sits clearly inside the rim
  4. Click Re-detect Colonies
Wide Rim / False Edge Colonies in Agar Dilution analysis mode

In full-plate (agar dilution) analysis, the plate rim often produces bright artefacts that are mistaken for colonies. This is the most common cause of inflated counts in agar dilution mode.

Fix: Reduce the Plate Radius slider by 5–15 pixels until the false rim colonies disappear from the overlay, then click Re-detect Colonies. Apply the same adjustment consistently across all plates in the same batch.

Re-opening Saved Sessions

Every image processed through the manual review workflow has its session saved automatically in editing_sessions/ inside your output folder. You can reload any session to review or redo it.

To Load a Saved Session

  1. Go to Tools → Load Editing Session
  2. Navigate to your output folder → editing_sessions/
  3. Select the *_session.json file for the image you want to review
  4. The editor opens showing the image with all previously saved colony annotations
  5. Make any corrections, then use Continue to re-save
Session Files
Session files (*_session.json) store all colony positions, classifications, and boundary parameters from the last editor save for that image. They do not include the image itself the original image file must be accessible at its original path (or in the input directory).

Re-runs and Result Overwriting

Always Use a New Output Directory for Re-runs

ColonyPy updates colony_analysis_results.csv (disk diffusion) or agar_dilution_results.csv (agar dilution) by overwriting rows for any image that is re-processed. If you re-run with the same output directory, your previous results for that image are replaced with no confirmation prompt.

To preserve all versions of your results:

  1. Create a new output folder before each re-run (e.g. run2_adjusted_boundary/)
  2. Set this as the output directory in the Setup tab
  3. Run analysis as normal

Batch summary (BATCH_SUMMARY_*.csv) and replicate statistics (REPLICATE_STATISTICS_*.csv) files are timestamped and never overwritten. A new file is created each time analysis completes.

Output Files

FileDescription
colony_analysis_results.csvMaster results table for disk diffusion runs (one row per image, including the matched control plate for each strain). Updated each time an image is processed. Delete this file or use a new output directory before re-running.
agar_dilution_results.csvMaster results table for agar dilution / population analysis profiling runs (one row per image, including the matched control plate for each strain). Kept separate from colony_analysis_results.csv so it only contains columns relevant to the agar dilution method, control plates that precede an agar dilution batch are written here rather than to colony_analysis_results.csv. Same overwrite policy as above.
{image}_analysis.pdfPer-image annotated visualisation. Disk diffusion includes ZOI regression plot. Agar dilution shows full plate with colony overlay and stats box.
BATCH_SUMMARY_{timestamp}.csvSummary across all images in the batch. New file created each run.
REPLICATE_STATISTICS_{timestamp}.csvGroup statistics with CV warnings. Groups are formed by strain + condition. Minimum 2 replicates per group required.
colony_sizes.csvPer-colony size data for every image that has been saved through the Manual Editor. Each row is one colony with its area, classification, and source image. Written only after a manual save, always reflects the reviewed colony list, never raw automated detections.
editing_sessions/{image}_session.jsonSaved editor state for each manually reviewed image. Used by Load Editing Session.
Two Separate Results CSVs

ColonyPy writes to one of two CSV files depending on which analysis method the batch used: disk diffusion results (and their control plates) go to colony_analysis_results.csv, while agar dilution results (and their control plates) go to agar_dilution_results.csv. This keeps each file's columns relevant to that method, agar dilution has no disk or zone-of-inhibition geometry, so those columns are simply not present in agar_dilution_results.csv rather than appearing as empty N/A columns throughout. Running a mixed batch (some images disk, some agar dilution) in the same output directory produces both files, each containing only the rows for its own method.

Trained StarDist Model

The bundled StarDist model was trained specifically on fungal colony images from the Nielsen Laboratory. Understanding the model architecture and training conditions helps you get the best results and interpret detection limitations correctly.

Architecture

ParameterValue
ArchitectureStarDist2D U-Net backbone
Input channels1 (single-channel grayscale)
Ray count32 (star-convex polygon approximation)
U-Net depth3

Two-Stage Accuracy

The model achieves approximately 80% automated recall. After manual review using the editor (adding missed edge colonies, removing false positives), effective accuracy reaches 95–99% for well-prepared plates. This is why the manual review workflow is recommended for published results.

Training Image Conditions

All training images were acquired under these exact conditions:

  • Light application: Coomassie Blue
  • Imager: Bio-Rad ChemiDoc, white transillumination mode
  • Exposure: 0.9 seconds (standard; only adjust if contrast is poor with your specific media, see Imaging Requirements)
  • Size: Medium 1830 × 1646 pixels, 300 DPI, 24-bit colour, 15.5 × 12.4 cm
  • Plate: Standard 90 mm petri dish

The model is expected to perform best on images that closely match these conditions. Images from different imagers, different exposure times, or different lighting protocols may give reduced accuracy.

Image Preprocessing Pipeline

Before StarDist runs, each image goes through the following pipeline:

  1. Unsharp mask sharpening (disk diffusion only) amount = 1.5, sigma = 5.0 px. Applied to colour image before grayscale conversion.
  2. Grayscale conversion
  3. CLAHE contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalisation (clip limit 3.0, 8×8 tile grid)
  4. Reference standardisation intensity profile matched to the training dataset mean and standard deviation
  5. StarDist normalisation percentile stretch before model inference. Standard mode uses the 1st–99.8th percentile. When Enhanced Detection is enabled, the upper percentile is lowered to 95th, which boosts dim or small colonies at the cost of compressing the intensity range of larger colonies.

Troubleshooting

Disk not detected / disk detection failed

ColonyPy uses a Hough circle transform to find the disk. This fails if:

  • The disk is at the very edge of the frame, ensure the full plate is visible
  • The tray has smudges or bright spots near the disk size range
  • The image is very dark or overexposed, check you are using 0.9 s. If contrast is genuinely poor for your media type, adjust within the 0.8–1.5 s range and compare to the reference images in the Imaging Requirements section

If detection fails, ColonyPy will ask if you want to skip the image. Use the Manual Editor to open the image directly and set the disk position manually.

False colonies detected on the plate rim

The inner surface of the petri dish rim often produces a bright ring of artefacts. To fix:

  1. Open the editor for the affected image
  2. Reduce the Plate Radius slider until the green boundary circle sits inside the rim
  3. Click Re-detect Colonies
  4. Apply the same radius adjustment to all plates in the batch for consistency
Fewer colonies detected than expected near the ZOI edge

Colonies at the outer edge of the ZOI are often lower contrast and may be missed by automated detection. This is normal, the model has ~80% automated recall. Use manual review to add missed edge colonies:

  1. In the editor, select Add Tolerance or Add Heteroresistance mode
  2. Click on each missed colony
  3. Alternatively, expand the ZOI boundary slightly using the ZOI slider and Re-detect
Lawn in the ZOI

If colonies have grown into a confluent lawn, ColonyPy cannot count individual colonies. The model is designed for convex, colonies only. Solutions:

  • Repeat the experiment with a lower inoculum concentration
  • The lawn colony clusters will be detected as single large heteroresistance colonies, this is not biologically meaningful and should not be included in analysis
StarDist not installed / model not found

This should not occur with the PyInstaller executable as StarDist and the model are bundled inside. If you see this error:

  • Re-download the ColonyPy executable the download may have been corrupted
  • Ensure you are running the correct executable for your platform (Windows .exe, macOS .app, Linux binary)
  • On macOS, make sure you extracted the .zip fully before launching do not run directly from inside the zip

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use images from a different imager?

The StarDist model was trained on images from a Bio-Rad ChemiDoc with Coomassie Blue light application at 0.9 s exposure. Use 0.9 s as your standard. Exposure may be adjusted within 0.8–1.5 s only if you observe poor contrast with a specific media type, compare results to the reference images in the Imaging Requirements section before proceeding. Images from other imagers may have different contrast profiles that reduce detection accuracy. If you use a different system, we recommend validating manually on a representative subset of images before using results for publication.

Do I need a control plate for every strain?

Yes. The classification threshold is derived from the p25 (25th percentile) colony size on the matched control plate. Without a control plate, ColonyPy uses the default threshold (12 px by default), which is unlikely to be calibrated for your strain. Always include at least one control plate per strain per batch.

Can I analyse multiple plates per image?

No. ColonyPy expects one plate per image. Use the ChemiDoc imaging software to capture separate images for each plate.

What does the CV warning in replicate statistics mean?

CV (coefficient of variation) measures variability across replicates. A "HIGH VARIABILITY" flag appears when CV exceeds the threshold for that metric (e.g. 20% for total colonies). High CV may indicate: inconsistent inoculum between replicates, variable culturing, imaging artefacts, or biological variability. Investigate flagged groups before reporting.

How do I report ColonyPy in a methods section?

Suggested methods text:

Please cite the ColonyPy publication once it becomes available Atim et al., 2026 (when available). Colony images were acquired using a Bio-Rad ChemiDoc imaging system (white transillumination mode, 0.9 s exposure, Coomassie Blue light application; 1830 × 1646 pixels, 300 DPI, 24-bit colour, 15.5 × 12.4 cm physical size). Colony detection and classification were performed using ColonyPy v1.0 (Nielsen Laboratory), which implements a StarDist deep-learning segmentation model (F1 = 80.5%, precision = 82.9%, recall = 78.2%, trained on 60 images). Colonies were classified as Tolerance or Heteroresistance based on size relative to the p25 (25th percentile) colony area of strain-matched no-drug control plates. Automated detections were reviewed and corrected using the ColonyPy manual editor.
How do I save settings between sessions?

Use File → Save Settings… to save your current parameters (directories, method, colours, thresholds) to a JSON file. Load them again with File → Load Settings… at the start of your next session.
